title: Where were you, Krishna?
hookLine: Draupadi tells her friend Krishna that even he failed her, and he hears every word
carry: sakhya: you can tell God everything

cards: Chariots on a forest road. Word has reached Krishna's people that the Pandavas are in exile, and Krishna comes to find them. The cousins embrace.
Then Draupadi speaks, and she doesn't make small talk. She tells him everything: the hall, being dragged in by her hair, the laughter, the husbands who sat silent. She weeps as she speaks.
And under all of it is one question she doesn't quite need to say out loud. Where were you?

teach.b: Draupadi doesn't tidy her grief. She names each wrong, in order, to the one person she trusts to hear it whole.
In the epic's telling, she gives him four reasons he should protect her: they're family, her dignity, his power to help, and one more word worth holding onto, sakhya, their friendship.
Then the hardest thing: she has no husband, no son, no brother, not even Krishna, because none of them protected her. Krishna, whom devotees worship as God, doesn't scold her.
He makes her a promise: the women of those who wronged her will one day weep as she is weeping now. Then, turning to Yudhishthira, he answers the question underneath.
Had I been in Dvaraka, I would have come to that game uninvited and stopped it.
But he was away, fighting a king named Shalva, who had attacked his city.
Draupadi speaks to Krishna as a friend, and in Hindu devotion that's a real way to love God. It's called sakhya: friendship with God.
In the Bhagavata Purana, the boy Prahlada lists nine ways of devotion, and friendship is one of them; devotees often name Draupadi and Arjuna as its great examples. A friend can say the hard thing.
So many Hindus feel free to bring God everything: grief, anger, even 'where were you?' Many teachers read the scene that way: devotion isn't only polite praise.
Honest words, said to God and heard all the way through, are prayer too.

how: Devotees revere Krishna as God, and storytellers dwell on this forest meeting, where Draupadi pours out her grief to her friend; sakhya, loving God as a friend, is counted among the classic ways of Hindu devotion.

s: Draupadi told Krishna that even he had not protected her
in the epic she counts him among those who failed her, and he doesn't argue.
Krishna told Draupadi to calm down and forgive
he listened, and promised that those who wronged her would answer for it.
sakhya, loving God as a friend, is one of the classic ways of Hindu devotion
Prahlada names it among nine ways of devotion in the Bhagavata Purana; devotees often point to Draupadi and Arjuna.

games.q: a friend says real devotees never complain to God; prayer is only for praise and thanks. by today's story, what's closer to Hindu teaching?
o: honest grief is welcome: Draupadi told Krishna even he failed her, and he listened.
she's right: Draupadi was punished for speaking that way.
complaints should go to a priest, never to God.
games.why: Krishna didn't scold her; he made her a promise. in sakhya, loving God as a friend, the hard words are part of the love.

practice: If you have a home shrine, sit before it; if not, anywhere quiet will do. Tell God, Krishna, or the holy as you know it, one true thing you've been holding back: a hurt, a disappointment, a 'where were you'.

Say it plainly, in your own words, the way Draupadi spoke to her friend. Then stay a few breaths and let yourself be heard. If you don't pray, say it to the quiet, or write it down, and let it be heard all the way through.

wordCard.voice: Vana. The forest of exile, where Draupadi tells her friend Krishna everything, and he hears it all.

orig.note: Sanskrit sakhya: friendship; in bhakti, loving God as a friend.

carryVoice: Your line: sakhya: you can tell God everything. Draupadi did, and Krishna heard her to the end. Tomorrow: is forgiving always right? Day seven hundred seventy-eight, done.
